2.0.s.en: 1. The prophet awaits the Lord's answer:

2.0.0.en: "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer concerning my complaint!" [1].

2.0.1.en: Many questions often turn in our thoughts, and it befits us not only to present them to the Lord but also to stand as on a watchtower awaiting the Lord's answer to us. We stand as on a fortress, reassured by faith and sure confidence that God, the Lover of mankind, does not hide His mysteries from us and does only what is for our edification. Thus the prophet, after presenting his question, stood on the watchtower awaiting the voice of the Lord within him, and on the fortress took refuge in it, so that the question would not turn into a shaking of faith. This watchtower and this fortress are none other than the person of our Lord Jesus: through Him we understand the sublime divine mysteries as though from a sublime watchtower, and in Him we find refuge, for He is the true Rock upon which the Church was founded and in which she takes shelter. He is the watchtower without whom we do not know the Father, as He says: "Neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whom the Son will reveal him" (Mt 11:27). And He is the Rock in which the Church takes refuge like a gentle dove, to whom He calls: "O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice" (Song 2:14).

2.0.2.en: St. Jerome sees that when Habakkuk stands as on a watchtower to watch and take his stand, and takes refuge as in a tower, he does so as a spiritual soldier who struggles against the devil without surrender. He contemplates the works of God and His mysteries, especially the Cross, and is filled with strength for the spiritual war against evil.

2.1.s.en: 2. The Lord's concern for the question:

2.1.0.en: 2 And the LORD answered me, and said, "Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it. 3 For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.

2.1.1.en: As long as the soul seeks and stands to watch for the words of the Lord and His answers, taking refuge in Him as in a fortress, taking its stand for spiritual striving through divine knowledge, He in turn does not withhold from it. The prophet says: "And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it. For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry" [2-3].

2.1.2.en: It is as though the Lord requires of him not to come to Him with a pen and paper to write what he sees and hears, but that there is need of tables on which the word of God is engraved in a clear script that draws the one who looks at it, so that he comes running to it... Moreover, the clarity of the script enables even those who are running to read it. In Isaiah it is said: "Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever" (Isa 30:8). Moreover, the vision may not be fulfilled immediately but at the appointed time, in the fullness of time; therefore it befits the prophet to wait, confident that it will surely come, even if it seems to be delayed.

2.1.3.en: What is this vision of which he speaks here, if not the one concerning the mystery of the Cross, which is fulfilled in the fullness of time when the Word of God becomes incarnate? He recorded divine love, not with ink and paper, but with His shed blood, and drew it on the two tables of the Cross, or its two beams, the vertical and the horizontal, drawing all to Himself.

2.1.4.en: Let us run in the Holy Spirit to the Cross to read what the Only-Begotten Son has engraved, declaring to us the sublime divine mysteries! Here we do not find the wicked Chaldeans perishing; rather, the devil himself and all his demons have utterly collapsed, and every authority they had usurped has been shattered.

2.2.0.en: When the Lord lifts up His prophet Habakkuk to the vision of the Cross, which shatters the kingdom of the devil, He goes on to reveal the works of the devil in the life of the wicked Chaldeans, which the Cross shatters. It is as though He reveals to us the evil planting which the Father did not plant but which is the sowing of the enemy of good, of which the Lord said that it must be uprooted (Mt 15:13). These evil plantings which He shatters are:

2.3.0.en: 4 "Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith. 5 Yea also, wine is treacherous; the man is proud, and does not rest. He who has enlarged his desire as hell, and is as death, and cannot be satisfied, but gathers unto him all nations, and heaps unto him all people: 6 Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say, Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay! 7 Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and awake that shall vex thee, and thou shalt be for booties unto them? 8 Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee; because of men's blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein.

2.3.1.en: "Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith. Yea also, wine is treacherous. The proud man does not rest" [4-5].

2.3.2.en: Although God permitted His people to be disciplined by means of the pagan Chaldeans, the Chaldeans became arrogant and thought that they had conquered and triumphed by their own power and might. Therefore God accomplishes His purpose through them, namely the discipline of His children, and then returns to punish them for the pride of their heart. As it was said by Isaiah the prophet concerning Assyria, that it is the rod of God's anger and the staff in their hand is His indignation (Isa 10:5), He accomplishes His purpose through them... "Wherefore it shall come to pass, that when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks. For he saith, By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom; for I am prudent: and I have removed the bounds of the people, and have robbed their treasures, and I have put down the inhabitants like a valiant man: and my hand hath found as a nest the riches of the people: and as one gathereth eggs that are left, have I gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved the wing, or opened the mouth, or peeped. Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it? as if the rod should shake itself against them that lift it up, or as if the staff should lift up itself, as if it were no wood" (Isa 10:12-15).

2.3.3.en: This is the work of the devil in the life of man... pride, so that man thinks that by his own power and wisdom he accomplishes his purpose, and does not realize that every energy and possibility is from God, even if man distorts its nature and turns it away from its purpose.

2.3.4.en: By pride the devil fell from his angelic rank and descended to the depths of the abyss (Isa 14:12; Obad 4); therefore he does not cease to strike humanity with the same disease, to bring it down with him from the life of faith, to make it lose the enjoyment of the divine Kingdom, and to cast it down to a level beneath the animal. St. John Chrysostom says: [He who exalts himself in his thought, lofty above men, is found lower than the irrational creation].

2.3.5.en: If the wicked man perishes through satanic pride, "the just shall live by his faith."

2.3.6.en: Scholars see that this phrase, "the just shall live by his faith," is the heart and sinew of Habakkuk's prophecy, and as it has been said, "these famous words sum up the whole vision." The Apostle Paul quoted it to affirm that justification is not possible by the works of the Law but by faith in Christ Jesus, as we are hidden in His righteousness. St. Augustine says: [In Him we rise, and in Him we go forth to the Father, to become perfect in an invisible way and justified]. Righteousness is not a collection; it requires sound faith that is not deviant, and as St. Augustine says: [Where there is no sound faith there is no righteousness, for the just shall live by faith].

2.3.7.en: Let us return to the pride which the enemy of good sows in us to deprive us of the true life of faith and to remove us from the righteousness that is in Christ Jesus. We find that this empty pride gives the soul a kind of inner hunger or thirst, through which man seeks to be satisfied not from the righteousness of God but from everything earthly, through injustice and plunder... and the more he receives, the more his inner emptiness increases, so that he remains unsatisfied all the days of his life.

2.3.8.en: In this spirit the Chaldeans attacked the nations, hunted humanity and humiliated them, without true satisfaction: "He who enlarged his desire as hell, and is as death, and cannot be satisfied, but gathers unto him all nations, and heaps unto him all evils; shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say to him that increaseth that which is not his, How long?! and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay: Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and awake that shall vex thee, and thou shalt be for booties unto them?! Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee; because of men's blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein" [5-9].

2.3.9.en: If we take the literal interpretation, we say that the Chaldeans enlarged their souls like the grave, swallowing peoples like the dead and never being satisfied. They were in continual motion to plunder nations and peoples by injustice without ceasing. But this work has an end; the balances are overturned and the captive nations are set free, to stand in mockery of the Chaldeans and to deride them, saying:

2.3.10.en: "Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long?"... They pour woes upon the Chaldeans, who thought they had gained much, but in truth it is not theirs; they are returning what they had counted as spoil!

2.3.11.en: "That ladeth himself with thick clay" (pledges)... What they gathered is not wealth but thick clay; it is not gold and silver, but they gathered dust that weighs down their souls with the love of the earthly world.

2.3.12.en: "Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and awake that shall vex thee?" In a moment the Chaldeans do not expect, while they are utterly secure, those who were as though asleep rise up, so that the Chaldeans become booty for them, after the Chaldeans had earlier taken them as booty. As they spoiled the nations, the nations spoil them; as they shed blood, their blood is shed; and as they wrought havoc on the land and the cities, havoc is wrought on them.

2.3.13.en: The matter does not stop at the satiety of the Chaldeans; rather, they lose what they thought was a gain for them, and they lose their wealth and their dignity... It is said to them: "As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head" (Obad 15).

2.3.14.en: If man thinks that sin, with its lusts and pleasures, satisfies the soul, in truth it brings him into a state of inner emptiness, hunger and thirst... So man runs to it to drink from it as from the salt waters of the sea, which increase his thirst and even make him lose his very life.

2.4.0.en: "9 Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil! 10 Thou hast consulted shame to thy house by cutting off many people, and hast sinned against thy soul. 11 For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it" [9-11].

2.4.1.en: This is the second woe. The first was because of the sin of pride, which does not satisfy the soul but destroys it; the second is because of the love of evil gain. The wicked man thinks that he fills his house with good things, and does not realize that he is gathering evil gain that brings a curse upon his whole house. The wise man says: "He that is greedy of gain (the covetous) troubleth his own house" (Prov 15:8). He gathers evil gain, reckoning that it will fly him to where no one can approach him, so that he builds his nest on high, but he finds that he is building his house with shame, and so he sins against his own soul. The stones he acquired with the money of injustice to build the house cry out, witnessing to his evil, and the wooden beams by which the building holds together do not keep silent. The house that he builds with the money of injustice turns into a sorrowful instrument that sings a lament over its owner.

2.4.2.en: King Ahab and his wife Jezebel thought that they had killed Naboth the Jezreelite and inherited his vineyard, with no one to question them and no one to watch their conduct, but they only acquired their own destruction, for the word of the Lord to Ahab through Elijah the prophet was: "In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine" (1 Kgs 21:19).

2.5.0.en: "12 Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity! 13 Behold, is it not of the LORD of hosts that the people shall labour in the very fire, and the people shall weary themselves for very vanity? 14 For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea" [12-14].

2.5.1.en: This is the third woe, which falls upon the man who, in his love of evil gain or ugly profit, turns into a ravening beast, so that he builds his city by shedding blood and establishes his town by the law of iniquity. St. John Chrysostom says: [Man has become worse than the wild beasts, for they do not eat one another so long as they are of the same kind; but man devours his brother in humanity, and thinks that he cannot build a city in which to rest except at the expense of his brother's blood!]

2.5.2.en: In any case, the earth is filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord when the world sees that the unjust shedders of blood have labored not to raise cities or establish towns but to become fuel for the fire, laboring in vain until sickness strikes them from exhaustion, and to no profit!

2.5.3.en: If our bodies, through shedding blood or through their iniquity, have become earth, then, when they receive the sanctification of the Spirit, they are filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord and bear the meek Spirit of their Savior; and if our life has become a salt sea, the sweet waters of the Holy Spirit transform its nature.

2.5.4.en: Finally, if injustice reaches its utmost ugliness when man becomes a shedder of blood, St. Jerome sees that the heretics are the worst shedders of blood: they do not kill the body but the souls, by deviation from the living faith, that is, from the truth, for he says: [The lying heretic kills many souls by deceiving them... He is a deceiver and thirsty for blood].

2.6.0.en: 15 "Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that pourest out thy wrath and makest him drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness! 16 Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the LORD's right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory. 17 For the violence of Lebanon shall cover thee, and the spoil of beasts, which made them afraid, because of men's blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein.

2.6.1.en: "Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that pourest out thy wrath and makest him drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness! Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the LORD's right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory" [15-16].

2.6.2.en: The fourth woe is for the sin of drunkenness. The one who becomes drunk, finding that he has lost his true dignity and inner balance, offers it to his companion, pouring out the bottle for him in order to tempt him by its sight, so that, as he himself has lost his purity, he wants to look on the nakedness of his brother, that is, his inner secrets, in order to corrupt him in his depths.

2.6.3.en: Who is the one who offers drunkenness if not the enemy of good, who draws man with his enticements as though he were his companion, in order to make him lose his true Christ and put him in a state of shame? This conduct does not add glory to the enemy but shame; if he thinks that by it he establishes his kingdom and widens its bounds, he only fills the cup of God's wrath against himself, to drink of the bitterness that he offered us, doubled: "in the cup which she hath filled fill to her double" (Rev 18:3, 6).

2.7.0.en: "Shameful spewing shall be on thy glory" [16]. Thus those around him look at him and find in him no true glory and no sincere wealth, so they vomit upon his vain glory! Thus the one who gives others of the intoxication of sin is only preparing for himself one who will vomit on him and shame him!

2.7.1.en: What we say about the intoxication of sin, to which the devil draws us, we say also about the life of luxury and indulgence, the life that carries within it the death of the soul and shame instead of outward glory. As St. John Chrysostom says: [The man who lives in pleasures is dead while he is alive, for he lives only for his belly... Is not he who spends his time in banquets and drunkenness dead, and buried in darkness?!].

2.8.0.en: "18 What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols? 19 Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise!

2.8.1.en: Shall it teach? Behold, it is laid over with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in the midst of it. 20 But the LORD is in his holy temple:

2.8.2.en: let all the earth keep silence before him" [18-20].

2.8.3.en: This is the last woe, which was directed against the Chaldeans, who boasted in their gods, which are the work of their hands. Truly they reveal cleverness in craftsmanship and skill in work, and they spent much to set them up, for they are overlaid with gold and silver, but inside they are stones, without spirit or life!

2.8.4.en: What will these idols profit them on the day of their punishment?! They asked the enemy, that is, the wooden Baal, to awake and save them, and the stone goddess Ashtoreth, the wife of the god Baal, to take heed of what had befallen them and to take pity on their condition, but neither is able to save. They are two gods fair to look upon but utterly powerless, whereas the true God is in His holy temple, and the earth cannot stand before Him.

2.8.5.en: Strange is the man who leaves his God, who dwells in his heart as in a heavenly temple, and pursues his own thoughts as though they were pagan gods, beautiful in appearance and shining, but lifeless and unable to offer salvation.

2.9.0.en: Wretched is the man who rejects the Giver of salvation, who makes of his heart a heaven, and worships deceitful human thoughts and philosophies, which make of him earth... He cannot resist the Lord when he hears the voice: "Let all the earth keep silence before him" [20].

2.9.1.en: May we not be earth that is silent and dumb before God, but a spiritual heaven that bears the word of God, joyful heavenly voices, and an angelic hymn that never ceases.
